strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for speech and NLP: whether Mamba can serve as a reusable self-supervised speech encoder. Combining ASR fine-tuning, four SUPERB tasks, efficiency measurements, and representation analyses provides a useful empirical perspective.

The causal Base results are promising: Mamba achieves 15.77% WER versus 16.66% for the causal Transformer while using fewer parameters. Table III also shows substantial improvements in phoneme recognition and speaker identification, including a parameter-matched Mamba+MLP comparison.
Document-level ExtBiMamba improves WER from 13.37% to 11.08%. The reported paired significance test provides some supporting evidence that longer context benefits this model.

The authors retrain Transformer baselines under the same stated pretraining budget and report unfavorable results transparently. The bidirectional architecture ablations and weaker Base-scale results make the study more informative than a uniformly positive comparison.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate for a clear Findings recommendation. Section III does not explicitly identify the pretraining corpus or provide model dimensions, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, masking configurations, or sufficient pseudo-label construction details. ASR fine-tuning and decoding settings are also missing, and Section IV-C does not clearly identify its dataset or evaluation split. No accompanying code or configuration release is specified.

The streaming claim exceeds the demonstrated evidence. A causal backbone and a WER comparison do not establish an end-to-end streaming recognizer. The paper does not document causality or lookahead throughout the feature extractor, positional processing, and downstream head, nor evaluate incremental decoding, state caching, chunk sizes, or emission latency. Whole-sequence inference timing does not resolve these questions.

The efficiency evidence needs correction and stronger controls. Figure 1's RTF axis runs from approximately 400 at the top to 1800 at the bottom, with Mamba having larger numerical values than Transformer, contradicting the text's claim of lower RTF. The metric definition or labeling must be clarified. Moreover, OOM with an explicitly materialized causal attention mask is implementation-dependent; without reporting attention kernels, precision, batch size, and memory-efficient attention controls, it does not establish a general Transformer limitation.

The long-context comparison is insufficiently specified and controlled. The retained dataset sizes, evaluation split, duration distribution, and treatment of test talks are unclear. Training and evaluation segmentation change together, making it difficult to isolate the source of improvement. The paired t-test lacks the pairing unit and sample size, and the claimed improvement on repeated rare words has no supporting examples or quantitative analysis. A practical chunked or memory-efficient Transformer baseline would strengthen the comparison.

Several conclusions are broader than the results warrant. At matched Small-scale parameter counts, causal Mamba has worse phoneme recognition and essentially the same aggregate score as the causal Transformer; Base bidirectional ExtBiMamba loses on all four tasks. These are useful findings, but they support task- and configuration-dependent tradeoffs rather than general superiority or an established architectural scalability limitation. Seeds or uncertainty estimates are absent for these comparisons.

The representation analyses are not sufficiently reproducible, and their application claims remain indirect. The datasets, phone alignments, clustering samples, and CCA fitting/evaluation procedures are unspecified. Higher phone purity or correlation with another model's embeddings does not establish better spoken-language-model units or stronger downstream representations, especially given the weaker bidirectional probing results. No spoken language modeling experiment tests the asserted benefit. Together with the methodological gaps above, this warrants revision before acceptance rather than rejection on grounds of limited novelty.

strengths: The study addresses a relevant question for speech NLP: whether Mamba can provide reusable self-supervised representations while supporting efficient long-context and causal recognition. Combining ASR fine-tuning, four SUPERB tasks, and representation analyses gives the exploration useful breadth.

The reported results are promising in specific settings. ExtBiMamba improves from 13.37% to 11.08% WER with document-level processing, with a reported paired-test p-value of 0.001. Causal Mamba achieves 15.77% WER versus 16.66% for the causal Transformer while using fewer parameters.

Retraining Transformer baselines under the same reduced pretraining schedule is a useful control. Parameter-matched comparisons and bidirectional architecture ablations strengthen the study, and the paper openly reports the substantial underperformance of base-size bidirectional Mamba.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient for a clear Findings recommendation. Section III does not identify the pretraining corpus or provide essential architecture configurations, optimization settings, masking parameters, and pretraining clustering settings. ASR fine-tuning and decoding procedures are underspecified, and the causal-ASR dataset and evaluation split are not explicitly identified. The representation analyses omit their datasets, sample sizes, alignment procedure, and CCA fitting/evaluation protocol. References to HuBERT and SUPERB do not resolve these experiment-specific omissions.

The empirical efficiency evidence needs correction and stronger controls. Figure 1 labels its right axis as RTF, but the plotted values decrease with sequence length and are higher for Mamba, whereas the text says RTF increases with length and is lower for Mamba. These may be inverse-RTF measurements, but the metric is not defined sufficiently to tell. Moreover, OOM for a particular masked-attention implementation does not establish an unavoidable Transformer limitation; attention backend, precision, batch size, and memory-efficient attention comparisons are missing.

The streaming-ASR claim exceeds the demonstrated evidence. Table II establishes a WER comparison between nominally causal backbones, but the paper does not establish end-to-end causality of the feature extractor and downstream head or report incremental decoding, state handling, lookahead, or emission latency. Full-sequence timing in Figure 1 does not substitute for a streaming evaluation.

The document-level result is encouraging but does not isolate the benefit of long-range context. Training and evaluation segmentation change together, and the paper does not clearly establish matched retained data or explain boundary handling and scoring. A context-length ablation or matched segmentation control would help distinguish context benefits from other protocol changes. The paired test lacks the pairing unit and sample size, and the claimed improvement on repeated rare words has no examples or quantitative analysis.

Several conclusions generalize beyond the measurements. Higher peak phone purity supports a narrow claim about phonetic clustering, not demonstrated benefits for spoken language modeling. CCA similarity to pretrained speaker or emotion embeddings is also a proxy rather than direct evidence of superior attribute representations. The probing results are mixed: base bidirectional ExtBiMamba loses on every task, and parameter-matched small causal Mamba does not improve the aggregate score. Calling this a scalability limitation is tentative without controlling architecture and optimization across scales.

Uncertainty is inadequately characterized outside the document-level comparison: ASR and probing results lack confidence intervals or repeated-run variation, making modest improvements difficult to assess. Overall, the topic and preliminary evidence merit revision, but missing experimental specifications and unresolved efficiency and streaming claims prevent acceptance on soundness and reproducibility grounds. These issues appear addressable in a next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for speech representation learning: whether Mamba can provide efficient, reusable alternatives to Transformer-based HuBERT. Its combination of ASR fine-tuning, four SUPERB tasks, and representation analysis offers useful empirical breadth.

The causal results are promising. Mamba achieves 15.77% WER versus 16.66% for the causal Transformer with fewer parameters, and the parameter-matched Mamba+MLP improves phoneme recognition and speaker identification in Table III.
Document-level ExtBiMamba improves WER from 13.37% to 11.08%, with a reported paired-test p-value of 0.001. This provides encouraging evidence for exploiting longer context.

Training Transformer baselines under the same reduced-budget setup supports comparison fairness. The paper also transparently reports negative results, including the base-sized bidirectional Mamba's weaker probing performance, and investigates alternative bidirectional designs.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient for a clear Findings recommendation. Section III does not explicitly identify the pretraining corpus or provide complete model configurations, optimization settings, masking and clustering settings, or absolute batch sizes. ASR fine-tuning and decoding protocols are underspecified, particularly the dataset and evaluation split for Table II. No code or configuration release is provided.

The efficiency evidence contains a consequential inconsistency. Figure 1 labels its runtime metric as RTF, but its inverted vertical axis shows values decreasing with input length and numerically higher values for Mamba, whereas the text claims increasing RTF and lower values for Mamba. The metric definition, units, and plot need correction before the measured speed advantage can be assessed.

The Transformer OOM comparison does not establish an architectural inability to process long recordings. Attention kernels, precision, batch size, and memory-management settings are unspecified, and the causal-mask explanation suggests implementation-dependent overhead. An optimized memory-efficient attention baseline and explicit peak-memory measurements are needed to substantiate the practical advantage.

Causal ASR accuracy alone does not demonstrate streaming performance. The paper does not document end-to-end causality of the feature extractor and downstream components, state caching, chunking, lookahead, or emission latency. Full-sequence runtime measurements cannot resolve these issues.

Statistical support is limited. Most comparisons have no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals. The long-context paired test omits its sample size and pairing unit, and the training-budget and evaluation controls needed to isolate the effect of context are unclear.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Phone purity and CCA similarity are useful diagnostics but do not establish improved spoken-language-model performance or attribute disentanglement. The analysis datasets, alignment procedure, and CCA estimation protocol are also unspecified. General causal superiority should be qualified: the matched-size small Mamba loses on phoneme recognition and aggregate score, while base-sized Mamba loses on emotion and intent classification.

Overall, the empirical direction is worthwhile, but missing reproducibility details and unresolved efficiency and streaming claims prevent acceptance in the current form. These appear addressable through focused documentation, corrected measurements, and targeted validation, supporting resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for speech representation learning: where Mamba can offer practical advantages over Transformer-based HuBERT. Its combination of ASR fine-tuning, representation analysis, architectural ablations, and downstream probing provides useful empirical breadth.

The causal Base results are promising. Mamba achieves 15.77% versus 16.66% ASR WER with fewer parameters, while the parameter-matched Mamba+MLP improves phoneme recognition and speaker identification. Appendix E extends evaluation to ten SUPERB tasks and shows that these advantages are accompanied by task-specific tradeoffs.

The document-level experiment demonstrates a useful capability: ExtBiMamba improves from 13.37% to 11.08% WER when trained and evaluated on longer context. The paper also reports negative results transparently, including weaker bidirectional Base performance and training instability.

Training Transformer baselines under the same reduced-resource pretraining regime helps control comparisons. Multiple cluster counts and comparisons between internal and external bidirectional designs provide additional supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The claimed no-lookahead streaming setup is insufficiently established. Section 3 preserves HuBERT's convolutional frontend and positional convolution, but does not explain how their padding, normalization, and future context are made causal. Masking attention or using a causal Mamba backbone alone does not establish end-to-end causality. Section 4.3 reports offline test-clean WER without incremental decoding, state-caching details, or emission latency. An explicit causality audit and actual streaming evaluation are needed to support a central claim.

The efficiency comparison establishes advantages over the tested implementation, but does not establish the broader practical conclusions. Transformer OOM is attributed partly to materializing a causal mask; memory-efficient attention and cached or chunked inference are not evaluated. Figure 1 also labels values in the hundreds to thousands as RTF, with a reversed vertical axis and trends that do not clearly match the stated interpretation. The timing definition, units, precision, batch size, synchronization, and attention implementation need clarification.

Reproducibility is inadequate for several key experiments. The abstract's code-availability statement has no URL. Model depths, widths, and Mamba state/expansion settings are not fully specified; the added 12-layer convolutional encoder and long-context fine-tuning configuration are insufficiently described. The representation analyses omit dataset/split details, alignment provenance, clustering sample sizes, and CCA fitting/evaluation procedures. Referring generally to HuBERT defaults does not resolve these custom choices.

The long-context result needs stronger controls and reporting. Filtering talks longer than 20 minutes changes the evaluation set without reporting retained counts or durations. Training and evaluation context change together, so the gain does not isolate inference-time use of distant context. The paired t-test lacks its pairing unit and sample size, and the claimed improvement in repeated rare words is unsupported by examples or targeted measurements.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Phone purity measures phonetic cluster alignment, not general quantized-unit quality or demonstrated usefulness for spoken language modeling. Correlation with speaker embeddings does not establish disentanglement. Likewise, two model sizes, a tenfold learning-rate change for bidirectional Base models, and mixed-precision instability do not isolate an architectural scalability limitation.

All training results come from single runs, leaving uncertainty around modest ASR and aggregate-score gains. There is also a reproducibility inconsistency: Appendix C defines the four-task aggregate using slot filling, whereas Tables 3–5 and Section 6 use intent classification. These concerns, together with the unresolved streaming and efficiency protocols, warrant revision before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant empirical question for speech processing: when Mamba can replace Transformer backbones in HuBERT. Combining ASR fine-tuning, representation analysis, architectural ablations, and downstream probing provides useful breadth.

Retraining Transformer baselines under the same reduced-data-exposure setup improves comparability. The parameter-matched causal comparison is particularly useful: Mamba+MLP improves phoneme recognition and speaker identification, and Appendix E confirms advantages across several additional tasks.
The document-level ASR result is promising: ExtBiMamba improves from 13.37% to 11.08% WER, with a reported paired-test p-value of 0.001.

The paper reports unfavorable results transparently, including weaker bidirectional Base performance and deficits on emotion and semantic tasks. These observations could support a useful empirical contribution without requiring architectural novelty.
weaknesses: The central streaming claim is insufficiently established. Section 3 preserves HuBERT's feature extraction and convolutional positional encoder, but does not explain how their padding, normalization, and future context are handled. Standard HuBERT preprocessing is not automatically causal when attention is masked or replaced. Consequently, Section 4.3's claim of no lookahead requires an explicit end-to-end causality audit. Offline test-clean WER also does not establish streaming latency or incremental decoding performance.

The efficiency evidence has a material reporting inconsistency. Figure 1's RTF axis runs from approximately 400 at the top to 1800 at the bottom; Mamba has numerically larger values, and values decrease with sequence length. This contradicts the text's statements that Mamba has lower RTF and that RTF increases with length. The metric definition, units, and timing procedure need correction. Moreover, OOM for the chosen dense-attention implementation establishes a practical limitation of that baseline, not a general Transformer limit; a memory-efficient attention comparison is needed to substantiate the broader claim.

Important reproduction details are missing: model dimensions and state sizes across configurations, the appended 12-layer convolutional encoder, task-specific fine-tuning schedules and decoding, and data selection and fitting procedures for phone purity and CCA. The abstract's code-availability statement has no URL. Referring to default HuBERT settings does not specify these departures from HuBERT.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Higher phone purity alone does not establish better units for spoken language modeling, which is not evaluated. CCA similarity to pretrained speaker embeddings measures alignment with those embeddings rather than directly demonstrating disentanglement. Bidirectional scalability conclusions are also confounded by the tenfold lower Base learning rate and observed numerical instability; two model sizes under different optimization conditions provide limited evidence of an architectural scaling limitation.

Uncertainty is inadequately characterized. Results come from single training runs, and most comparisons have no confidence intervals. The long-context paired test omits the pairing unit and sample count, while document-level training and evaluation change together, limiting attribution specifically to broader context. Small aggregate probing gains should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

The aggregate-score protocol is inconsistent: Section 6 and Tables 3–5 use intent classification as the fourth task, whereas Appendix C specifies slot filling. This needs resolution to reproduce the reported scores. Overall, the causal validity, efficiency reporting, and methodological omissions prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present; focused implementation checks, corrected reporting, and additional controlled evidence could make a next-cycle revision viable.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for speech representation learning through a useful combination of ASR fine-tuning, SUPERB probing, efficiency measurements, and representation analysis.

Retraining Transformer baselines under the same reduced-data-exposure pretraining setup improves comparability. Parameter-matched configurations and architectural ablations further strengthen the empirical study.
The causal results are promising: Mamba achieves 15.77% versus 16.66% WER with fewer parameters, while the full SUPERB evaluation supports improvements in several phonetic and speaker-related tasks.

Document-level ExtBiMamba improves WER from 13.37% to 11.08%. The paper also candidly reports weaker bidirectional Base results and investigates training instability rather than presenting uniformly positive findings.
weaknesses: The claimed no-lookahead streaming setup is not established. Section 3 retains HuBERT's convolutional positional encoder without explaining how it is made causal; the standard encoder accesses future frames. Frontend normalization and convolutional buffering also require clarification. Causal backbone masking alone does not demonstrate end-to-end causality, and no actual streaming latency or incremental decoding evaluation is reported.

Reproducibility is insufficient for several central experiments. The code link in the abstract is missing, model dimensions and Mamba state/configuration details are unspecified, and the added 12-layer ASR convolutional encoder lacks architectural details. Fine-tuning schedules, decoding settings, retained TEDLIUM split sizes, and the datasets/alignment procedures for phone purity and CCA are also inadequately documented.

The practical efficiency conclusion depends on an inadequately characterized Transformer implementation. No memory-efficient exact-attention baseline is evaluated, so OOM does not establish that comparable Transformers cannot process the documents. Figure 1 also labels values around 400–1800 as RTF, with Mamba numerically higher than Transformer, contradicting the prose claiming lower RTF. The metric definition and timing protocol need correction or clarification.

Evidence for robustness is limited. Results use one training run, several aggregate-score gains are small, and the reported long-context paired t-test does not identify its pairing unit or sample size. The tenfold lower learning rate for bidirectional Base models and observed numerical instability also complicate attributing poorer performance to architectural scalability.

Some conclusions exceed the measurements. Higher phone purity does not establish better spoken-language-model performance, and correlation with pretrained speaker embeddings does not establish disentanglement. Appendix C additionally specifies slot filling where the main four-task evaluation uses intent classification, leaving the aggregate-score computation inconsistent.

The contribution is promising, but the unresolved causality, efficiency-reporting, and reproducibility issues affect central claims and prevent a sound Findings recommendation. These appear addressable through focused clarification and additional experiments in a next-cycle revision.
